sections.COMMENTS: ï»¿This seismogenic source was first proposed by Blumetti et al. (1993) based on geological evidence. Following the 24 August 2016, Mw 6.0, Amatrice earthquake a few scattered breaks were reported along the Mt. Gorzano primary bedrock fault scarp.Â The breaks were interpreted by some investigators as evidence for primary slip along the underlying seismogenic fault.Â No ruptures were observed following the Mw 5.5-5.4, Campotosto earthquakes of 18 January 2017. Given this contrasting evidence we see no reason to modify the assignment of the Mt. Gorzano fault to the Debated source category.

pictures.c: Stereogram (not to scale) showing  geomorphic features of the Mt. Gorzano fault escarpment. The main fault trace is highlighted in red. Notice the offset of various remnants of the "Villafranchian" surface (from Blumetti et al. [1993], modified).

pictures.c: Tectonic features of the Amatrice-Campotosto basin grouped on the basis of their geomorphic expression (from Cacciuni et al. [1995]).

Sketch-map showing relationships between the instrumental location of the 1950 earthquake, the isoseismal lines and the main tectonic features of the Amatrice zone (from Di Filippo and Marcelli [1951]).

pictures.t: Cross-section from Di Filippo and Marcelli [1951]
pictures.c: Geological section across the epicentral zone of the 1950 earthquake. Notice the proposed epicentral location and the geometry of the Mt. Gorzano fault at depth (from Di Filippo and Marcelli [1951]).

pictures.t: Geological map from Bachetti et al. [1990]
pictures.c: Geologic, geomorphic, structural features in a narrow belt along Mt. Gorzano fault. A-A': section across the fault (see cross-section). Notice the location of 37 ka tilted palustrine deposits (from Bachetti et al. [1990]).
Geological section across the Mt Gorzano fault zone (see A-A' in the Geological map). Notice the location of tilted palustrine deposits (6) dated at 37 ka (from Bachetti et al. [1990]).
